title: Say who said it (Avot 6:6)
hook: quoting in the name of the one who said it brings redemption, as Esther did
tomorrow: a whole book of Talmud, start to finish. where do you even begin?

segments.voice: Yesterday, forty-eight ways to acquire Torah, with a listening ear near the top. The very end of that same list holds one more.
screen: `A LISTENING EAR.` → `THE LAST OF THE FORTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: A friend says something brilliant at lunch. Two days later you post it, word for word, and it gets more likes than anything you've ever written. Nobody asks where it came from. So whose line is it now? The last of Avot's forty-eight ways answers that, and it attaches a surprisingly big promise.
screen: `A FRIEND'S LINE. YOUR POST.` → `NOBODY ASKS.` → `WHOSE LINE IS IT NOW?`

segments.voice: Avot says: whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it brings redemption into the world. The proof comes from the book of Esther. Mordecai overhears two guards plotting to kill the king. He tells Esther, and Esther tells the king, in Mordecai's name. Why would credit bring redemption? Two readings live in the tradition, and they pull different ways. The first follows the plot. Because Esther named Mordecai, his deed was written in the king's book of chronicles. Later, on a sleepless night, the king has that book read to him, finds Mordecai's name, and honors him, and the story turns toward rescue. On this reading, credit is a seed: a name written down at the right moment changes what happens next. The second reading follows the speaker. The Talmud says that when a teaching is repeated in a sage's name in this world, his lips move in the grave. On this reading, credit isn't about outcomes at all. It keeps a person in the conversation, still speaking after they're gone. One reading looks at what credit does for the future. The other, at what it owes the past. The tradition keeps both. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud's tractate of blessings, where this path goes tomorrow, says things like, Rabbi Avin bar Rav Ada said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak. Two names, so neither one goes quiet.
screen: `SAY IT IN THE NAME OF WHO SAID IT.` · `ESTHER TELLS IT IN MORDECAI'S NAME.` · `READING ONE: CREDIT IS A SEED.` · `READING TWO: THE LIPS STILL MOVE.` · then, large: `SAY WHO SAID IT.`

segments.voice: Think of one line you repeat as your own: a phrase, a kitchen trick, a piece of advice. Trace it back to whoever first said it to you, and say their name out loud, once, along with the line. Then keep them in mind for the rest of the sit.
screen: `ONE LINE YOU REPEAT.` · `WHO SAID IT FIRST?` · `SAY THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Say who said it. The last of Avot's forty-eight ways: repeat a teaching in the name of the one who said it.
For the road: say who said it, and the name keeps speaking. That's Avot, finished.

howItsDone: In Jewish study it's customary to cite a teaching with its chain of names, 'so-and-so said in the name of so-and-so', and many teachers credit even a student's insight by name.

fork.setup: you lean toward reading one: credit matters because of what it sets in motion. now give reading two its best case.
options: naming a teacher keeps them speaking; credit is owed to the past, whatever it changes.

original.note: Hebrew: whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule against copying.
what it means: naming the source brings redemption into the world; Esther's credit to Mordecai was recorded and later turned the story.
what a scholar hears: the same saying, with the same Esther proof, appears in the Talmud at Megillah 15a; Yevamot 97a adds that a sage's lips move in the grave when he's quoted.

speak the name of God aloud before you begin to learn
introduce yourself by name before you speak in class

chat.says: posted saba's old pharmacy joke. it kinda blew up. everyone thinks it's mine. does that matter??
options: It matters. Avot says: say who said it. Put Saba's name on it.
Not really. Once a joke is out there, it belongs to whoever tells it.
Only if Saba asks. Credit is his to claim, not yours to hand out.
chat.meaning: The last of Avot's forty-eight ways: say a thing in the name of the one who said it. Either reading, Saba gets named.

Avot.meaning: Pirkei Avot, the Mishnah's book of sages' sayings

Esther.meaning: the Jewish queen of Persia in the book of Esther

Mordecai.meaning: Esther's cousin, who uncovered a plot against the king

Talmud.meaning: the Mishnah with the rabbis' long discussions of it

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 6:6 (whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it brings redemption into the world)
Esther 2:21–23; 6:1–3 (the plot told in Mordecai's name; written in the chronicles; the sleepless king)
Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 97a (a sage's lips move in the grave when a teaching is said in his name)
Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 15a; Berakhot 6a (the saying with the Esther proof; 'Rabbi Avin bar Rav Ada said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak')
